title: Destined to Collide
caption: The Triangulum Galaxy, Messier 33, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Data obtained and processed by: P. Massey (Lowell Obs.), G. Jacoby, K. Olsen, & C. Smith (AURA/NSF) · Image processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab), A. Hussein (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This view from the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory shows the Triangulum Galaxy, also called Messier 33. Almost 3 million light-years from Earth, it is a close neighbor of the Andromeda Galaxy.

Triangulum is the third-largest member of the Local Group, the gathering of galaxies that includes the Milky Way and its nearest neighbors, of which Andromeda is the largest. The two share a history, though astronomers are still working out the details. Because they are so close, some researchers suggest Triangulum is a satellite of Andromeda, much as the Moon is a satellite of Earth, only on a vastly larger scale.

Others propose they are independent galaxies that have simply grazed each other, pointing to streams of stars and neutral hydrogen gas that link them. Whatever the case, the two will probably collide in 2.5 billion years, merging and eventually evolving into a lenticular galaxy.
scale: The Triangulum Galaxy lies almost 3 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic I camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through broadband U, B, V, R and I filters plus narrow [O III], S II and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
